summary: Help 7-8 year olds move from 'fraction = part of a shape' to 'fraction = a number with a place on the line'. The load-bearing idea: a fraction 1/b is made by splitting ONE unit (the distance between two whole numbers) into b equal SEGMENTS, which needs b−1 marks between them, and a/b is the point at the end of the a-th equal segment counted from 0 (for a less than b, this is the a-th interior mark). Keep the unit visible so children stop treating the whole line as the unit and stop placing 3/4 'between 3 and 4'. Core model is a 0-to-1 line partitioned into equal segments; progress to landmark lines and then unmarked lines to force interval thinking, and use dual labelling to show equivalence as the same point.
misconceptions: Treats the number line like a ruler — counts tick marks (or draws 4 marks for fourths) instead of equal segments (IES Roadblock 2.1)
Places 3/4 between 3 and 4, treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers (IES Roadblock 2.2)
Treats the whole line as the unit — e.g. locates 3/4 three-quarters of the way across a 0-to-5 line
Sees a fraction only as part of a shape, not as a single number that has a place on a line

activities.title: Three marks make fourths: partition and place on an interactive line
steps: On a 0-to-1 line, set a 'cut this unit into ___ parts' control to 4 and watch exactly THREE marks drop in, splitting the line into four equal segments.
Say aloud how many marks made four parts (three, not four), and colour each of the four segments, counting SEGMENTS rather than marks.
Drop a bead on the third mark; if the line reports a fraction, check it announces '3/4' and explain why that point is 3/4.

Extend the line from 0-to-1 to 0-to-4, keeping each whole-number unit the same length (or redraw it that way), and notice the 3/4 bead stays three-quarters of the way from 0 to the first '1', nowhere near the '3'.
On a second track below, lined up with the same 0 and 1 and labelled in tenths, slide a 1/2 bead until it lands exactly on 5/10, and state that the two labels name the same point.
activities.insight: A fraction 1/b comes from cutting one unit into b equal segments (needing b−1 interior marks), and a/b is the point at the end of the a-th segment. The unit stays 'one whole' even when the line gets longer, so 3/4 lives between 0 and 1, not between 3 and 4. Equivalent fractions are the same point under different labels.

activities.title: Place and reason on paper lines: pre-marked, landmark, then unmarked
steps: On a 0-to-1 line already divided into four equal segments (fourths), place 1/2, 1/4 and 3/4 by counting equal segments from 0.

On a minimally-labelled line showing only 0, 1/2, 1, 1½ and 2, place a concrete fraction such as 1¾ using landmarks — reasoning that it sits just below 2 (between 1½ and 2) — rather than counting every mark.
On an UNMARKED 0-to-1 line, decide how many segments you need, make the b−1 marks yourself, then place the fraction.
Answer landmark-reasoning questions such as 'Is 1/12 closer to 1/4 or to 0?' and 'Is 3/4 closer to 0 or to 1?', explaining using distance.
On a 0-to-4 line, place both 3 and 4, then separately place 3/4, and say in your own words why 3/4 does not go between 3 and 4.
activities.insight: Placement is driven by magnitude and distance from landmarks, not by counting ticks. Children who can partition an unmarked line themselves have internalised that the unit is divided into equal segments, and they keep fractions within the correct whole-number interval.

activities.title: Bridge from the shape model and compare unit fractions
steps: Shade 3/4 of a fraction strip exactly as long as the 0-to-1 unit, starting the shading at one end, then lay that end at 0 along the line so the shaded part reaches a point; name that point as the number 3/4.
Partition one unit into thirds, then partition an identical unit into eighths, and compare the lengths of a single segment in each.
Place 1/3 and 1/8 on the same 0-to-1 line and decide which is further from 0, explaining using segment length.
State in your own words whether a fraction such as 3/4 is 'a number' or 'just a piece of a shape', and point to where it lives on the line.
Reference check: label 0, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4, 1 on a line and explain for each point which segment's end it marks.
activities.insight: A fraction names one number and has a single location on the line; the area (shape) model and the length (line) model agree. More equal parts of the same unit means each part is smaller, so 1/8 is closer to 0 than 1/3 — the denominator counts how many parts split ONE whole.

checkQuestion: First, look at this number line from 0 to 1. There are three marks spaced equally between 0 and 1, and I have put a dot on the third mark. What number is at the dot, and how do you know? Now here is a fresh line labelled from 0 to 4. Put 3/4 on it, and put 1/2 on it, and tell me why each one goes where you put it.
checkAnswer: The dot is at 3/4, because 0-to-1 is divided into four equal parts (segments) and the dot sits at the end of the third part. On the 0-to-4 line, 3/4 goes three-quarters of the way from 0 towards 1 (just below 1, NOT between 3 and 4) and 1/2 goes halfway between 0 and 1; each is a single number between 0 and 1 because its denominator splits ONE unit.
